feed.subtitle: Diagram-first design walkthroughs of automations, DevOps, and cloud infrastructure by Allan Niñal. Open to builds, collabs, and design reviews.

entry.title: A tax rate updater on AWS for a few dollars a month
entry.summary: Keeps a register of the tax rates your business has hard-coded, watches the official sources, and tells a person before a change lands. AWS, about $2 a month. Part 1 of 7 in the Tax rate updater series.

entry.title: How the rate register works
entry.summary: Building the list of every rate your business has written down, why the "used in" column is the whole point, and how to find the rates nobody remembers. Part 2 of 7 in the Tax rate updater series.

entry.title: How a source gets read
entry.summary: Fetching a government page without breaking on every redesign, why the snapshot is kept, and why a source that stops being readable is an alarm rather than silence. Part 3 of 7 in the Tax rate updater series.

entry.title: How a rate change gets dated
entry.summary: Announcement and effect are months apart, and the gap is the whole value. Reading the effective date, handling changes with no date, and the transitional cases. Part 4 of 7 in the Tax rate updater series.

entry.title: How the rate reminder works
entry.summary: The second notice before the effective date, the per-place checklist, and why acknowledging is the only interaction the system ever asks for. Part 5 of 7 in the Tax rate updater series.

entry.title: What the tax rate updater costs
entry.summary: About $2 a month at 600 checks. Where every cent goes, which line grows with volume, and the three ways this bill could surprise you. Part 6 of 7 in the Tax rate updater series.

entry.title: Engineering reference: the tax rate updater architecture
entry.summary: The tax rate updater drawn for engineers: service names, region, the Lambda inventory, IAM scopes, DynamoDB schemas and the Bedrock model id. Part 7 of 7 in the Tax rate updater series.

entry.title: An invoice dispute triager on AWS for a few dollars a month
entry.summary: Classifies each dispute into one of six standard reasons, gathers the evidence that reason needs, pauses chasing, and hands a person a decision. AWS, about $3 a month. Part 1 of 7 in the Invoice dispute triager series.

entry.title: How a dispute gets recognised
entry.summary: Telling a dispute apart from a question, a payment remittance and an out-of-office — and why stopping the chaser happens before anything is understood. Part 2 of 7 in the Invoice dispute triager series.

entry.title: How a dispute gets classified
entry.summary: Six reasons, one model call, and why "I cannot tell" is a better answer than a confident wrong one — because a wrong class gathers the wrong evidence. Part 3 of 7 in the Invoice dispute triager series.

entry.title: How the evidence gets gathered
entry.summary: What gets pulled for each of the six reasons, why narrow beats complete, and the one-screen summary that turns a folder of documents into a decision. Part 4 of 7 in the Invoice dispute triager series.

entry.title: How a dispute decision gets recorded
entry.summary: Resuming the chaser, the record a resolved dispute leaves, and the monthly report that turns individual disputes into one fixable process problem. Part 5 of 7 in the Invoice dispute triager series.

entry.title: What the invoice dispute triager costs
entry.summary: About $2 a month at 40 disputes. Where every cent goes, which line grows with volume, and the three ways this bill could surprise you. Part 6 of 7 in the Invoice dispute triager series.

entry.title: Engineering reference: the invoice dispute triager architecture
entry.summary: The invoice dispute triager drawn for engineers: service names, region, the Lambda inventory, IAM scopes, DynamoDB schemas and the Bedrock model id. Part 7 of 7 in the Invoice dispute triager series.

entry.title: A subscription audit bot on AWS for a few dollars a month
entry.summary: Finds recurring charges in the card feed, groups them into subscriptions with an owner and a purpose, and asks one question before each renewal. AWS, about $3 a month. Part 1 of 7 in the Subscription audit bot series.

entry.title: How the transaction feed arrives
entry.summary: Three ways a card feed turns up, why a read-only feed is the hard boundary, and how re-uploading last month's export does not double every charge. Part 2 of 7 in the Subscription audit bot series.

entry.title: How charges become a subscription
entry.summary: Grouping on interval rather than name, the four patterns worth recognising, why annual subscriptions are the hard case, and what a broken pattern usually means. Part 3 of 7 in the Subscription audit bot series.

entry.title: How a subscription gets an owner
entry.summary: Three ways to attribute a subscription, why an unowned one is the most valuable finding, and how the merchant string becomes an actual product name. Part 4 of 7 in the Subscription audit bot series.

entry.title: How the renewal question works
entry.summary: One question per subscription per year, timed to land before the renewal, with what was said last time — and why asking more often destroys the system. Part 5 of 7 in the Subscription audit bot series.

entry.title: What the subscription audit bot costs
entry.summary: About $2 a month at 120 new merchants. Where every cent goes, which line grows with volume, and the three ways this bill could surprise you. Part 6 of 7 in the Subscription audit bot series.

entry.summary: The subscription audit bot drawn for engineers: service names, region, the Lambda inventory, IAM scopes, DynamoDB schemas and the Bedrock model id. Part 7 of 7 in the Subscription audit bot series.

entry.title: A utility bill watcher on AWS for a few dollars a month
entry.summary: Reads every utility bill as it arrives, compares usage, unit rate and standing charge against your history and your contract, and mentions only what moved. AWS, about $3 a month. Part 1 of 7 in the Utility bill watcher series.

entry.title: How a utility bill gets read
entry.summary: Two lanes in, Textract on a page that every supplier lays out differently, and the three numbers plus a meter number that come out — or do not. Part 2 of 7 in the Utility bill watcher series.

entry.title: How a bill gets matched to a meter
entry.summary: Why the meter number on the page is a hint rather than an answer, the three-step match, and what a bill for an unknown meter actually means. Part 3 of 7 in the Utility bill watcher series.

entry.title: How a change gets reported
entry.summary: One message per bill, naming which of the three numbers moved and by how much — and why the distinction between usage, rate and standing charge is the whole message. Part 4 of 7 in the Utility bill watcher series.

entry.title: How the utility history builds
entry.summary: The row every bill writes, why estimated readings never become the baseline, and the three things a couple of years of clean history lets you do that you cannot do otherwise. Part 5 of 7 in the Utility bill watcher series.

entry.title: What the utility bill watcher costs

entry.summary: The utility bill watcher drawn for engineers: service names, region, the Lambda inventory, IAM scopes, DynamoDB schemas and the Bedrock model id. Part 7 of 7 in the Utility bill watcher series.

entry.title: A cash drawer reconciler on AWS for a few dollars a month
entry.summary: Compares the end-of-shift count with the till report, explains the variance from the day's own records, and surfaces only what is left. AWS, about $3 a month. Part 1 of 7 in the Cash drawer reconciler series.

entry.title: How a close gets recorded
entry.summary: A photo of the count sheet, a till report from wherever it comes from, and how the two get matched to the same shift without anybody typing a reference. Part 2 of 7 in the Cash drawer reconciler series.

entry.title: How a variance gets explained
entry.summary: Working through the day's own records for the missing money — cash refunds rung as card, no-sales, float changes, safe drops and tip-outs — before anybody is told a number. Part 3 of 7 in the Cash drawer reconciler series.

entry.title: How a cash pattern gets surfaced
entry.summary: The rolling window, the three patterns worth reporting, why a single shift never triggers anything, and the one case that skips the window entirely. Part 4 of 7 in the Cash drawer reconciler series.

entry.title: How a cash finding gets closed
entry.summary: Recording a cause against a till and slot, why a closed finding suppresses future reports, the monthly summary, and the two numbers that say whether the thresholds are right. Part 5 of 7 in the Cash drawer reconciler series.

entry.title: A timesheet validator on AWS for a few dollars a month
entry.summary: Checks each timesheet as it is submitted against the roster, the job records and your break and overtime rules, and asks the submitter about anything odd. AWS, about $3 a month. Part 1 of 7 in the Timesheet validator series.

entry.summary: A web form, a spreadsheet upload and a photo of a paper sheet, and how all three become one row per person per day — including what the reader refuses to guess. Part 2 of 7 in the Timesheet validator series.

entry.summary: Five checks against the roster, the job log and your rules tab — missing days, unmatched jobs, breaks, day length and the overtime threshold — and which of them can close a sheet alone. Part 3 of 7 in the Timesheet validator series.

entry.title: How a payroll week gets closed

entry.title: A mileage claim checker on AWS for a few dollars a month

entry.title: A supplier bill matcher on AWS for a few dollars a month
entry.summary: Matches every supplier bill against the purchase order and goods-received note line by line, and flags anything off. It never pays. AWS, about $3.20 a month. Part 1 of 7 in the Supplier bill matcher series.

entry.title: How a supplier bill gets read
entry.summary: Three ways a bill enters the matcher: an emailed PDF parsed by Textract, a supplier-portal poll, and a manual upload. One Bedrock call makes it clean lines. Part 2 of 7 in the Supplier bill matcher series.

entry.title: How a bill gets matched three ways
entry.summary: A plain-Python matcher checks item, quantity and price against tolerances across the bill, the PO and the goods-received note, and picks one of four outcomes. Part 3 of 7 in the Supplier bill matcher series.

entry.title: How a mismatch reaches the right person
entry.summary: Approver resolution per supplier, quiet hours, a second sign-off for big spend, an email naming the exact line and gap, and four guardrails on every flag. Part 4 of 7 in the Supplier bill matcher series.

entry.title: How a bill gets approved for payment
entry.summary: Three actions on every bill: approve with a reason if it overrides a flag, query the supplier, or reject. Every action is logged. No bill pays itself. Part 5 of 7 in the Supplier bill matcher series.

entry.title: What the bill matcher costs
entry.summary: A few dollars a month at SMB volume. The three-way match is free; the cost is Textract reading each bill and one small Bedrock call to clean the lines. Part 6 of 7 in the Supplier bill matcher series.

entry.title: Engineering reference: the bill matcher architecture
entry.summary: Resource names, IAM scopes, Bedrock model IDs, Lambda inventory, the SES inbound rule set, and the DynamoDB schemas for the supplier bill matcher. Part 7 of 7 in the Supplier bill matcher series.

entry.title: A weekly report builder on AWS for a few dollars a month
entry.summary: Gathers your own numbers — sales, new customers, cash, top items — compares them to last week and last month, and emails a short summary every Monday. Part 1 of 7 in the Weekly report builder series.

entry.title: How the numbers get gathered
entry.summary: Each source you list — a sales sheet, a Stripe or bank CSV, a point-of-sale summary — is mirrored to S3 on a schedule and read into one set of weekly figures. Part 2 of 7 in the Weekly report builder series.

entry.title: How the weekly report gets written
entry.summary: Plain Python computes every figure and comparison first. Only then does one Bedrock call turn those real numbers into a paragraph. It sources no figure itself. Part 3 of 7 in the Weekly report builder series.

entry.title: How the report reaches the owner
entry.summary: The Monday send: the right recipient, the owner's timezone, the report held until the data is complete, and four checks between the writing and the inbox. Part 4 of 7 in the Weekly report builder series.

entry.title: How a number that looks off gets flagged
entry.summary: Plain-Python checks catch a stale source, a figure outside its normal range, or a total that does not add up. Anything that trips is shown, marked unverified. Part 5 of 7 in the Weekly report builder series.

entry.title: What the weekly report builder costs
entry.summary: A couple of dollars a month at SMB volume. It runs weekly, gathers and compares in plain Python, and fires one Bedrock call to write the paragraph. Part 6 of 7 in the Weekly report builder series.

entry.title: Engineering reference: the weekly report builder architecture
entry.summary: Service names, resource identifiers, region, Bedrock model IDs, Lambda inventory, IAM scopes, the EventBridge Scheduler config, and the DynamoDB schemas. Part 7 of 7 in the Weekly report builder series.

entry.title: A content moderator on AWS for a few dollars a month
entry.summary: Checks every comment against your house rules, passes the safe ones, holds the clear breaches, and sends borderline ones to a human. AWS, about $2 a month. Part 1 of 7 in the Content moderator series.

entry.title: How a comment gets checked
entry.summary: Every comment, review or post arrives through one webhook, gets cleaned and stored, and a fast rule pass settles the easy cases before any model looks. Part 2 of 7 in the Content moderator series.

entry.title: How a comment gets a verdict
entry.summary: The rule pass settles most items alone. Only the borderline middle reaches Bedrock Haiku 4.5, which returns a call, a confidence score and the rule cited. Part 3 of 7 in the Content moderator series.

entry.title: How flagged content reaches a moderator
entry.summary: The review queue, who gets each area, quiet hours and batching so nobody is pinged at 2am, and four guardrails between a held verdict and the review card. Part 4 of 7 in the Content moderator series.

entry.title: How the moderator makes the final call
entry.summary: Three actions on the review card: publish releases a held item, remove takes it down with the reason logged, edit-and-publish does both. Overturns teach it. Part 5 of 7 in the Content moderator series.

entry.title: What the content moderator costs
entry.summary: A couple of dollars a month at SMB volume. The rule pass settles most items with no model; Bedrock fires only on the borderline middle and the digest. Part 6 of 7 in the Content moderator series.

entry.title: Engineering reference: the content moderator architecture
entry.summary: Resource names, IAM scopes, Bedrock model IDs, Lambda inventory, the SQS review queue, and the DynamoDB schemas for the content moderator. Part 7 of 7 in the Content moderator series.

entry.title: A shift scheduler on AWS for a few dollars a month
entry.summary: Drafts a fair weekly rota that respects availability and hours, publishes it once the manager approves, and routes swap requests to them. About $2.20 a month. Part 1 of 7 in the Shift scheduler series.

entry.title: How a shift week gets set up
entry.summary: Three ways a week enters the sheet: the Drive sheet, a time-off lane that reads plain-English requests into dates, and a template lane for standing shifts. Part 2 of 7 in the Shift scheduler series.

entry.title: How a fair rota gets drafted
entry.summary: A weekly run places people into shifts by rule, preferring whoever is furthest below their hours target, and picks one of four outcomes. Part 3 of 7 in the Shift scheduler series.

entry.title: How a schedule reaches the team
entry.summary: Manager approval first, then per-person delivery: quiet hours, calendar invites, a Slack DM of each person's own shifts, email fallback, four guardrails. Part 4 of 7 in the Shift scheduler series.

entry.title: How a shift swap gets approved
entry.summary: Three actions on a swap request: cover finds a qualified replacement, drop returns the shift to the open pool, time-off holds the day. A manager says yes. Part 5 of 7 in the Shift scheduler series.

entry.title: What the shift scheduler costs
entry.summary: Pennies a month for a small team. The drafter runs weekly with no model on the draft; Bedrock fires on time-off notes and the fairness summary. Part 6 of 7 in the Shift scheduler series.

entry.title: Engineering reference: the shift scheduler architecture
entry.summary: Resource names, IAM scopes, Bedrock model IDs, Lambda inventory, EventBridge schedules and DynamoDB schemas for the shift scheduler. Part 7 of 7 in the Shift scheduler series.
